function.description: Retrieve weather forecast data for a specified location and date range. The data includes temperature, precipitation, and wind speed. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

location.description: The location for which to retrieve the weather forecast, in the format of 'City, Country' (e.g., 'London, UK').

start_date.description: The start date for the forecast period in the format of 'YYYY-MM-DD' (e.g., '2023-04-01').

end_date.description: The end date for the forecast period in the format of 'YYYY-MM-DD' (e.g., '2023-04-07').

include_details.description: Whether to include detailed hourly forecast data or not. If set to false, only daily summaries will be provided.

message.content:
The sea typically looks **blue**—the same reason the sky does. Water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange) more strongly than shorter ones (blue, violet), so when sunlight hits it, the blue light is scattered back into our eyes. That’s why we see a deep blue over open ocean.

But the exact hue can vary:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water scatters less light, giving a darker, richer blue. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | Greenish tint; high concentrations make the water look green or even brown. |
| **Shallow coastal waters** | Often turquoise or aquamarine because they reflect more surface light and scatter less. |
| **Sun angle & time of day** | Early morning or late afternoon can give a golden or pinkish glow. |
| **Sediment & runoff** | Brownish or muddy tones if rivers bring silt or pollution. |

So while “blue” is the classic description, the sea’s color is actually a spectrum influenced by depth, biology, sediment, and lighting conditions.
